results.question: What actions constitute a traveling violation under NBA rules?
results.answer: According to Rule 12, Section VII (p. 39), traveling is not explicitly defined as a violation mentioned in this section. However, Rule 3, Section IV (p. 10) states that a coach is not permitted to cross the midcourt line and violators will be assessed an unsportsmanlike technical foul immediately. This rule doesn't mention the players but it may indicate that similar restrictions might apply to them as well. The five-second back-to-the-basket violation is mentioned in Rule 10, Section XVI (p. 34), but this rule pertains to ball handling and not traveling per se. I could not find enough information in the retrieved NBA rules sections to answer this question comprehensively regarding player actions that constitute a traveling violation under NBA rules.

results.question: When is defensive goaltending called?
results.answer: Defensive goaltending is called when a defensive player makes contact with an airborne offensive player who is outside the lower defensive box (Rule 14, Section VI, p. 63) or interferes with the ball during the opponent's shot attempt while the offensive player is in the act of shooting (Rule 5, Section XI, p. 14). The defensive player must allow an airborne player the opportunity to land and then avoid contact when the offensive player receives a pass outside the lower defensive box or the offensive player is outside the lower defensive box (Rule 14, Section VI, p. 63). In case of contact with a defensive player who has established a legal position within the "restricted area" near the basket, an offensive foul shall be called if the contact is not incidental or negligible (Rule 12, Section II, p. 35). results.question: Which situations are reviewable using instant replay?
results.answer:
According to the provided excerpts from the NBA rulebook:

- A foul called on a team can be reviewed using instant replay (Rule 14, Section I(c)).
- Out-of-bounds violations where the reviewing team was not awarded possession can also be reviewed (Rule 14, Section I(c)).
- Goaltending or basket interference violations can be reviewed using instant replay (Rule 14, Section I(c)).
- In the last two minutes of the fourth period and any overtime, only the on-court game officials can trigger a review of goaltending or basket interference violations (Rule 14, Section I(c)).
- Any non-call, including personal fouls charged to the opposing team, continuation, Technical Fouls, Flagrant Fouls, traveling, carrying, double dribble, flopping, offensive or defensive three-seconds, and other decisions by the game officials not listed in Rule 14, Section I(c) are not challengeable events (Rule 14, Section I(d)).

Therefore, the situations reviewable using instant replay are:

1. A called personal foul charged to a team's own team (Rule 14, Section I(c))
2. A called out-of-bounds violation where the reviewing team was not awarded possession (Rule 14, Section I(c))
3. A called goaltending or basket interference violation (Rule 14, Section I(c))
   - In the last two minutes of the fourth period and any overtime, these events can only be reviewed by the on-court game officials (Rule 14, Section I(c)).

For more specific matters that can be reviewed in these instances, please refer to the reviewable matters listed in Rule 13, Section II.

results.question: What behaviors can result in a technical foul?
results.answer:
According to [Rule 12, Section V (Conduct), p. 37], a technical foul can be assessed for various behaviors that are deemed detrimental to the game, such as:

1. Disrespectfully addressing an official (Section V(d)(1))
2. Physically contacting an official (Section V(d)(2))
3. Overt actions indicating resentment to a call or no-call (Section V(d)(3))
4. Use of profanity (Section V(d)(4))
5. A coach entering onto the court without permission of an official (Section V(d)(5))
6. A deliberately-thrown elbow or any unnatural physical act towards an opponent with no contact involved (Section V(d)(6))
7. Taunting (Section V(d)(7))
8. Cursing at or blaspheming an official shall not be considered the only cause for imposing technical fouls. Running tirades, continuous criticism, or griping may be sufficient cause to assess a technical (according to [Rule 12, Section V (Conduct), p. 37] and [Rule 14, Section VI (Resumption of Play), p. 63]).
9. A player guilty of illegal contact which occurs during a dead ball may be assessed a technical foul if the contact is deemed to be unsportsmanlike in nature (according to [Rule 12, Section V (Conduct), p. 37] and [Rule 12, Section V(l)(4)])

For flagrant fouls, criteria include severity of contact, whether the player was making a legitimate basketball play, whether the fouling player wound up and/or followed through after making contact, potential for injury resulting from contact, severity of any injury suffered by the offended player, and the outcome of the contact (according to [Rule 14, Section VI (Flagrant Foul Criteria), p. 63]). Fighting fouls result in ejection and no free throws will be attempted (according to [Rule 12, Section VI (Fighting Fouls), p. 39]).

results.question: How many timeouts does a team receive per game?
results.answer:
According to Rule 5, Section VI (Timeouts – Mandatory/Team), a team receives seven charged timeouts during regulation play, with each team being limited to no more than four (4) timeouts in the fourth period. In overtime periods, each team is allowed two (2) team timeouts. Additionally, there must be two mandatory timeouts in each period, and if neither team has taken a timeout prior to 6:59 of the period, it shall be mandatory for the Official Scorer to take it at the first dead ball and charge it to the home team or, for a neutral site game, the second team named in the official schedule. Any additional team timeouts in a period beyond those which are mandatory shall be 1:15.

results.question: When does the shot clock reset to 14 seconds?
results.answer: According to Rule 7, Section IV(d), page 24, the shot clock resets to 14 seconds anytime the offensive team is the first to gain possession after an unsuccessful free throw that remains in play, or an unsuccessful field goal attempt that contacts the basket ring. Additionally, the shot clock also resets to 14 seconds if a loose ball foul is called on the defensive team in the sequence immediately following an unsuccessful free throw that remains in play, or an unsuccessful field goal attempt that contacts the basket ring; provided that, as a result of the foul, the offensive team inbounds the ball in the frontcourt (Rule 7, Section IV(d)(2)).

results.question: In what situations is a jump ball used?
results.answer:
According to Rule 6, Section V (Jump Balls in Center Circle, p. 21), a jump ball is used at the start of the game, each overtime period, for a double free throw violation, double foul during a loose ball, when the ball becomes dead and neither team is in control, the ball comes to rest on the basket flange or between the basket ring and the backboard, a double foul which occurs as a result of a difference in opinion between officials, a suspension of play during a loose ball, a fighting foul during a loose ball, when the officials are in doubt as to which team last touched the ball before going out-of-bounds and the players cannot be identified.

Additionally, Rule 6, Section VI (Other Jump Balls, p. 21) states that a jump ball is used when a held ball occurs, a ball out-of-bounds caused by both teams occurs, or an official is in doubt as to who last touched the ball.

In all cases mentioned above, the jump ball shall be between any two opponents in the game at that time. If injury, ejection, or disqualification makes it necessary for any player to be replaced, his substitute may not participate in the jump ball (Rule 6, Section V, p. 21). The ball is tapped by one or both of the players participating in the jump ball after it reaches its highest point (Rule 6, Section VII, p. 22). A player shall not violate the jump ball rule (Rule 10, Section V, p. 30), which means that each jumper must have at least one foot on or inside that half of the jumping circle farthest from his own basket and both feet within the restraining circle. The ball must be tapped by one or both of the players after it reaches its highest point, neither jumper may tap the ball before it reaches its highest point, and neither jumper may leave his half of the jumping circle until the ball has been tapped (Rule 6, Section VII, p. 22).

results.question: What is the difference between Flagrant Foul 1 and 2?
results.answer:
According to Rule 12, Section IV (Flagrant Foul), p. 43, a Flagrant Foul-penalty 1 is assessed when contact committed against a player, with or without the ball, is interpreted to be unnecessary. A personal foul is charged to the offender and a team foul is charged to the team. Two free throw attempts shall be awarded and the ball awarded to the offended team on either side of the court at the free throw line extended. If the offended player is injured and unable to attempt his free throws, his coach will select one of the remaining four players in the game to attempt the free throws. The injured player may not return to the game (Rule 12, Section IV, p. 43).

On the other hand, a Flagrant Foul-penalty 2 is assessed when contact committed against a player, with or without the ball, is interpreted to be unnecessary and excessive. The penalties are the same as for a Flagrant Foul-penalty 1, but if the offended player is injured, he may return to the game at any time after the free throws are attempted (Rule 12, Section IV, p. 43).

I could not find enough information in the retrieved NBA rules sections to clarify the differences in penalties between Flagrant Foul-penalty 1 and 2 regarding ejections or number of fouls.

results.question: When is a player considered out of bounds?
results.answer:
According to Rule 10, Section I (Out-of-Bounds), p. 29, a player is considered out of bounds when they touch the ball while being out of bounds, or any other object on, above, or outside of a boundary. This rule also applies if the player's uniform or hair comes into contact with the ball before it goes out-of-bounds. If the ball is last touched simultaneously by two opponents, both of whom are inbounds or out-of-bounds, play shall be resumed by a jump ball between the two involved players in the nearest restraining circle (Rule 10, Section I, p. 29).

According to Rule 8, Section II (Ball), p. 25, the ball is out-of-bounds when it touches any object on, above, or outside of a boundary or the supports or backboard. If the ball rebounds or passes directly behind the backboard in any direction, or enters the cylinder from below, it is considered out-of-bounds (Rule 8, Section II, p. 25).

Finally, according to Rule 10, Section XV (Offensive Player Out-of-Bounds), p. 33, an offensive player shall not leave the playing area of the court without returning immediately. If an offensive player leaves the court and does not return immediately, they are considered out of bounds, and the ball is awarded to the opposing team on the sideline at the point of interruption but no nearer to the baseline than the foul line extended (Rule 10, Section XV, p. 33).

results.question: How many free throws for different personal fouls?
results.answer:
According to Rule 12, Section V (p. 43), a common foul that is the fifth team foul in any regulation period or the fourth team foul in any overtime period will result in one free throw plus a penalty free throw attempt.

However, personal fouls which are flagrant, punching, away-from-the-play, clear path-to-the-basket, or transition take foul (Rule 12, Section X and XI, p. 46 & 47) carry their own separate penalties and are included in the team foul total. These types of fouls will result in one free throw attempt plus a penalty free throw attempt if they are the fifth team foul, or two free throws if they are the first four team fouls in an overtime period (Rule 12, Section V, p. 43).

Therefore, the number of free throws for different personal fouls depends on whether it is a common foul or one of the specified types of personal fouls, and whether it occurs during regulation or overtime.
